row.name: East Ridge
row.description: A long ridge on the peak that towers over Moraine Lake, and a very different proposition from the walk-up tourist route on the other side. Rock quality varies from good to alarming, and the ridge is long enough that speed matters.

row.name: South Face
row.description: The highest summit entirely within British Columbia, deep in the Coast Mountains and a long way from a road. The rock and ice of the summit tower are the technical part; getting to the mountain and waiting out its weather are the rest of it.

row.name: Lotus Flower Tower
row.description: The southeast buttress in the Cirque of the Unclimbables — around two thousand feet of splitter granite, with the upper pitches following cracks up a clean headwall. Reaching it means a flight, a lake, and a long walk into the Mackenzies, which is most of why it stays as good as it is.

row.name: Northeast Buttress
row.description: A long, clean buttress on the shaded side of Slesse, close enough to the border that it is a familiar objective on both sides of it. Sustained moderate climbing at altitude-free elevation, with a descent that has caught out plenty of parties.
row.approach: Start at the Slesse Memorial trailhead on the Nesakwatch Creek forest road. The trail crosses Nesakwatch Creek on a bridge, follows an old logging road for part of the way, passes the memorial plaque and ends at the Propeller Cairn. Continue north over glacier-polished slabs, losing a little height toward a wooded ridge, and scramble a short gully (third to fourth class, often damp) to a notch in it. Drop into the cirque below the pocket glacier and climb slabs toward the head of the bowl, where the diagonal bypass ledge begins the route. Ice can fall onto these slabs from the glacier above, so cross the exposed stretch without stopping.
row.descent_text: The descent is long and is often the hardest part of the day. The usual way is the Crossover descent, which returns to the east-side trailhead with no car shuttle. From the summit it works down the west side of the summit ridge by cairned scrambling, a rappel from a slung block and a series of gullies and ledges (choosing the correct gully is critical) to the Slesse Mountain Trail. A cairn marks where the route leaves that trail for a notch, steep snowfields (bring an axe or at least crampons) and a contour around Mount Parkes to Crossover Pass. A rockslide damaged the old trail below the pass, so parties now rappel the bolted Crack of Noon Club route to talus, then follow cairns and flagging into the forest and rejoin the memorial trail. The alternative is the steep Slesse Mountain Trail down the west side, which ends at a different trailhead and needs a second vehicle; road access on that side has been restricted.

row.name: North Ridge
row.overview: Original 1931 line up the steep corner forming the Grand's right skyline from Jackson Hole; adventurous, moderate. Many variations exist. Icy chimney pitches are common except during prolonged high pressure in summer; the Italian Cracks are a popular alternative, and a finish on the Direct variation up the North Face adds technical climbing. Follow the easiest-looking way. P1: easy rock to a flake, squirm behind it (5.7). Gully to the Chockstone Chimney, the right wall has pitons, leading to the crux, a stem at 5.8. Next, 5.7 in the chimney of black rock, then the Slab Pitch, and a rightward line on Second Ledge to a corner that faces left, 2 or 3 pitches from the top. Much of it is 5.7.
row.approach: Four approaches reach the top of the Grandstand and the foot of the North Ridge. The Valhalla Traverse from the Lower Saddle is the standard and usually quickest. The Teton Glacier option (axe and crampons) adds glacier travel and route-finding; Mt. Owen via the Gunsight Notch involves tricky route-finding, unusual rappels and a 5.7 chimney; and the longest route goes up Cascade Canyon, crosses Cascade Creek into Valhalla Canyon and scrambles the west face of the Grandstand. Bivy spots include the Lower Saddle, the moraine below the Teton Glacier and near the top of the Grandstand.
row.descent_text: Descend the standard Owen-Spalding route to the Lower Saddle: one or two rappels with a single 60 m rope, combined with scrambling and some route-finding, bring you down. Sargent's Chimney is the first obstacle, followed by a rappel of about 120 ft to the Upper Saddle; from there avoid the first southeast gully and go west to the climbers' trails to the Lower Saddle, then down Garnet Canyon.
hazards: Overhead rockfall hazard on the glacier approach below the route
Chimney sections are commonly icy except during extended high-pressure summer stretches - verglas risk
10 pitches and 1,200 ft of climbing is long enough that afternoon storms are a real threat if the party is slow
Descent needs 1-2 rappels on the Owen-Spalding line followed by routefinding scrambles back to the Lower Saddle

row.name: Exum Ridge
row.overview: Rock route on the Grand Teton's southern spine. Key landmarks, low to high: Wall Street ledge (about 12,800', entered from the Lower Saddle), the Golden Stair, the Wind Tunnel gully, the Friction Pitch, the "V" dihedral and the Petzoldt lieback. Wall Street pinches down to a narrow, exposed finish, where the party should rope up. The Golden Stair has steep knobs and limited protection; the Friction Pitch is poorly protected; the "V" is very exposed but well protected. A couloir crossed on the approach drops from the Upper Saddle and cliffs out, so it is not a descent.
row.approach: From the Lupine Meadows trailhead, reached by Lupine Meadows Road just south of Jenny Lake, the Garnet Canyon trail climbs roughly 6.5 to 7 miles and about 5,000 ft to the Lower Saddle between the Grand and Middle Teton, passing the Platforms, Meadows and Caves camping zones on the way. The trail vanishes briefly across boulder fields, so take the path of least resistance and look for it again beyond. From the Lower Saddle follow the Owen-Spalding line left of the Needle pinnacle and up the gully close beside it, then diverge right and cross a wide, gentle couloir to reach Wall Street, a huge ledge at about 12,800 ft. Note that couloir for the descent, since it drops from the Upper Saddle and cliffs out. Wall Street is easy walking until it narrows and becomes exposed at its end, where parties rope up to start the Golden Stair pitch.
row.descent_text: Descend the upper Owen-Spalding route: downclimb Sargent's Chimney, then rappel about 120 ft onto the Upper Saddle. A single 60 m rope can do it from the slung horn if you angle to the right, though two ropes or a 70 m are more usual, and a shorter 70 ft rappel sits beside it; confident parties downclimb the 5.4 ground instead and skip the midsummer lines. The way down is hard to find, so note landmarks on the way up. From the Upper Saddle do not drop into the first gully heading southeast (the couloir below the saddle toward Wall Street cliffs out); work farther west to the climbers' trails that lead down to the Lower Saddle, then follow Garnet Canyon out to the Lupine Meadows trailhead.
hazards: Popular classic ridge — rockfall and traffic backups from parties climbing above are common
Two rappels required off the Upper Saddle before regaining the standard Owen-Spalding descent line
Long outing when linking Lower and Upper sections (roughly a dozen pitches) — afternoon thunderstorms are the main objective hazard
Route-finding on the ledge systems between pitches, especially through the Upper section

row.name: North Face Standard
row.overview: Climb along the right of the Teton Glacier (giant crevasses), then back left to the Grandstand base; crossing the bergschrund could cause trouble. Climb a few ropelengths up-right to the Guano Chimney, leading to the First Ledge, several hundred feet across at 20-40 degrees, usually with some snow. Traverse it up and right; trouble comes from snow, meltwater or verglas, and a party that met water over slabs stayed roped. From its right end climb steeply to the Second Ledge (5.6, as is the Guano Chimney). Cross the Second Ledge to the right and gain the Third Ledge, then up and right to the Pendulum Pitch; the Second Ledge can also be followed to the Owen Spalding as an escape.
row.approach: The route starts on the Teton Glacier, which is a real glacier with giant crevasses; climb the right side of it and then back left to the foot of the Grandstand. The bergschrund can be a problem. The route begins on the face left of the Grandstand base, climbing ledges and rubble, then trends up and right for several pitches to the Guano Chimney. Take an axe, and perhaps crampons, depending on conditions.
row.descent_text: The top section is the same as the North Face Highlight Tour and ends on easy ground near the summit. Descend the standard way: downclimb Sargent's Chimney, rappel about 120 ft to the Upper Saddle, then go west of the first southeast gully to the climbers' trails down to the Lower Saddle and Garnet Canyon.
hazards: Long, committing Grade IV route — parties need to move quickly given its length and weather exposure
Ice, snow, and rockfall are common on the First and Second Ledge traverses between pitches
Much harder to bail from partway than shorter routes like the North Ridge, which can be escaped after about 4 pitches
Afternoon thunderstorms are a serious concern on a route long enough to keep parties high on the face into the afternoon

row.name: Direct South Buttress
row.approach: Launch a canoe at String Lake, carry it over the short portage to Leigh Lake, and paddle across to the lake's far western corner, where Leigh Canyon opens out and campsite 14b sits. The overland route around the lakes is long, brushy and not maintained, which is why most parties paddle. A faint climbers' path starts on the north side of the campsite and runs up Leigh Canyon, with cairns that split into several paths across the talus. Climb the scree and talus toward Laughing Lion Falls, then go up the lower ramp, passing a stand of trees and curving beneath the blunt arete of the buttress to a gully at its base. The line follows the prominent buttress rising from the left end of the higher of two ramps that slant across the face left of the falls; two approach pitches link the lower ramp to it.
row.descent_text: The buttress ends in a bowl high on the south face, about a third of the way up the peak, and most parties descend from there. Many rappel from the east side of the bowl with double ropes, using trees and fixed anchors to reach the usual rappel line down the Blackfin chimneys and back to the ledges above Leigh Canyon. With a single rope you can instead follow the crest west to the end of the long horizontal section and take the couloirs that drop west toward the drainage between Moran and Thor Peak. To reach the summit instead, continue up the south ridge, or traverse east to join the CMC route and descend that. Early in the season an ice axe and crampons are useful.

row.name: Northeast Face
row.overview: Start early, since afternoon thunderstorms come from the southwest and stay unseen until they top the formation. Route finding is tested in a couple of places, and bailing after the first 300 feet is a challenge. Scramble the third-class ramp to sloping ledges, then the roofed dihedral and a 5.8 crack. Follow left-leaning ledge systems and cracks in dihedrals for at least 2 pitches; going right early dead-ends. Then go right to the 5.8 flare (5.9 3" variation), pass a large flake, finish with the crux, a short chimney holding a hand crack that rattles. Descent: 3rd class gully south, then 3 or 4 raps (two ropes recommended) to a ledge that leads left, to the descent used for South Buttress.
row.approach: From the Big Sandy trailhead, near 9,000 ft, take the Big Sandy trail (trail 99) past Big Sandy Lake and North Lake toward Jackass Pass; it is roughly 9 miles to Lonesome Lake. Above North Lake the trail steepens, and a cairned spur to the left leads toward Arrowhead Lake and the cirque, while the main trail crosses Jackass Pass (about 10,800 ft) and drops steeply to Lonesome Lake. For the northeast face, follow the trails on the north side of Lonesome Lake, keep left of the stream into the boulder field, then scramble left. Keep left of the foot of the curving ledge that turns into a long dihedral below a roof, gear up on the easy slabs, and go left up the third-class ramp to the first pitch.
row.descent_text: From the summit, scramble over and down the third-class gully on the south side to the top of the K Cracks on South Buttress. The standard way off is the South Buttress rappel line, which starts at the anchors at the top of the K Cracks and runs down climber's left of the route in three or four rappels of roughly 25 to 32 m. A single 70 m rope reaches the ledges, two ropes work as well, and a 60 m rope needs some easy low-fifth-class downclimbing, so watch the rope ends. From the lowest anchors, walk the broad ledge left to the south shoulder; there is a short class 2-3 section just before it.

row.name: East Ridge
row.overview: A narrow spine linking this summit to the neighboring tower, in places razor thin and elsewhere crowned with towers that are bypassed on exposed traverses. Most of it is fourth class, so roping all of it demands an early start, while moving unroped makes it quick. Famed for being clean, airy and photogenic, although some visitors grumble about the walk in, the way down and the shortage of hard moves.
